citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N_0)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], and let
$\nabla$ be its unique torsion-free $g$-compatible connection supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Fix a nonempty
connected open set $O\subseteq M$. A **selected stationary thermal carrier** on
$O$ consists of a smooth future timelike vector field $\xi$ and a smooth
positive scalar field $T:O\to(0,\infty)$, where $T$ is measured in kelvins,
such that $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-killing-field]]. Equivalently, the criterion is
$\nabla_{(a}\xi_{b)}=0$ by
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]. The round brackets mean
symmetrization with factor $1/2$. The choice of $\xi$ specifies the thermal congruence; no
coordinate chart or universal observer field is selected.

Set $N_\xi:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and $u:=\xi/N_\xi$. Then
$g(u,u)=-1$. In the length-coordinate convention $x^0=ct$, $u$ is
dimensionless and $cu$ is the physical four-velocity, with $c>0$ in
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in
$\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, define the inverse-temperature vector
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$, with units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, and the Killing-normalized
temperature field $T_K:=N_\xi T$. Thus $\beta=\xi/(k_BT_K)$; this definition
does not assert that $T_K$ is constant.

For a smooth chemical-potential scalar $\mu:O\to\mathbb R$ in joules, put
$\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$, a dimensionless scalar. Define the rest-space metric,
derivative, acceleration, expansion and shear by
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+u_au_b,\qquad D:=u^a\nabla_a,\qquad a_b:=u^a\nabla_au_b,\qquad \theta:=\nabla_au^a,\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}u_{d)}-\frac13\theta h_{ab}.$$
Here $a$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ have inverse-length units; the physical
proper acceleration is $c^2a$. The smooth tangent-bundle structure used by
the cited GR suppliers assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]; no stronger choice principle is part of this
definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The scalar $s:=-g(\beta,\beta)$ is smooth and strictly positive on $O$. Hence $s^{-1/2}$ is smooth and positive, so $T=(k_B\sqrt{s})^{-1}$ is a smooth positive kelvin-valued scalar and $u=\beta/\sqrt{s}$ is a smooth future-directed vector field. Direct contraction gives $g(u,u)=g(\beta,\beta)/s=-1$.

Lowering the smooth vector field $\beta$ with $g$ gives a smooth one-form, and its covariant derivative is a smooth covariant two-tensor. Antisymmetrizing this tensor gives the smooth two-form $\varpi$; the inverse-length derivative of the inverse-joule components of $\beta$ gives its stated units. Since $\mu$ and $k_BT>0$ are smooth, $\zeta$ and $\alpha=-\zeta$ are defined and dimensionless on all of $O$. The only foundational assumption in this construction is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in [F4]; no selection or stronger choice principle is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
(Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$,
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$ earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

derivations.claim: On each chartwise $C^1$ piece, $t\mapsto\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ is continuous because $\omega$ and the coordinate representative of $\gamma$ are continuous and the one-form evaluation is bilinear. Thus each displayed piece integral exists by [F1]. The covector-vector pairing has the same value after a chart change, so the integrand is intrinsically defined.

Any two admissible finite subdivisions have a finite common refinement. Repeatedly applying [F2] shows that subdividing a piece leaves the sum unchanged; hence the defined period is a unique real number independent of the chosen subdivision.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $\omega$ be a smooth real one-form on $M$, and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ curve with a finite subdivision into chartwise $C^1$ pieces and $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$. Define its oriented period by

$$\operatorname{Per}_\gamma(\omega):=\sum_j\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))\,dt,$$

where $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=1$ is any subdivision on whose pieces $\gamma$ is $C^1$. The covector-vector pairing is intrinsic, and additivity makes this value independent of further subdivision. No invariance under homotopy is asserted by this definition.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Fix the finite subdivision from [F1]. On each chartwise $C^1$ piece choose a chart containing the piece, write its coordinate curve as $x(t)$ and $\widetilde\phi=\phi\circ x^{-1}$. By [F2] the coordinate coefficients of $\omega$ are $\partial_i\widetilde\phi$; applying [F3] to $\widetilde\phi\circ x$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\phi\circ\gamma)(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on that piece. This derivative is continuous and therefore integrable by [F4].

Apply [F5] on each subdivision interval to $h=\phi\circ\gamma$. By [F1] the period is the sum of those integrals, so it equals the sum of the increments $\phi(\gamma(t_{j+1}))-\phi(\gamma(t_j))$. The internal endpoint terms cancel, and the remaining increment is $\phi(\gamma(1))-\phi(\gamma(0))=0$ because $\gamma$ is closed. Thus the period is zero.

boundaries.reason: If no closed curve is present the universally quantified claim is vacuous.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 yields the zero endpoint increment for every closed curve.

Let $O$ be a nonempty connected open subset of a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with its Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$ and length-coordinate convention $x^0=ct$. Let $\beta$ be a smooth future-directed timelike Killing vector field on $O$, with components in $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$, and fix $k_B>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K}^{-1}$. On $O$ define

$$T:=\frac{1}{k_B\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}},\qquad u:=k_BT\,\beta,\qquad \varpi_{ab}:=-\frac12(\nabla_a\beta_b-\nabla_b\beta_a).$$

Thus $T$ is in kelvins, $g(u,u)=-1$, and the covariant two-form $\varpi$ has units $\mathrm{J}^{-1}\mathrm{m}^{-1}$. For a smooth chemical-potential scalar $\mu:O\to\mathbb R$ in joules, set $\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$ and $\alpha:=-\zeta$, both dimensionless. These fields are defined only on the region where $\beta$ is future timelike; no thermal state or material realization is part of this definition.

Let $O$ be a connected open set in a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold, let $u$ be a smooth future unit timelike vector field on $O$
($g(u,u)=-1$), and let $T:O\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth. Define
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$, $h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+u_au_b$,
$D:=u^a\nabla_a$, $a_b:=u^a\nabla_au_b$,
$\theta:=\nabla_au^a$ and
$\sigma_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}u_{d)}-\theta h_{ab}/3$ as in
[[def-tgr-stationary-thermal-carriers]]. Then $\beta$ is a Killing field of
$g$ (equivalently $\nabla_{(a}\beta_{b)}=0$ by
[[def-gr-killing-field]] and
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]) if and only if
$$DT=0,\qquad \theta=0,\qquad \sigma_{ab}=0,\qquad h_a{}^b\nabla_b\log T=-a_a.$$
No hypersurface-orthogonality or vanishing-vorticity condition is assumed.

Use SI dimensions and the signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Take the geometric data of
[[def-tgr-stationary-thermal-carriers]]: $O$ is a nonempty connected open domain in a
smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$, $\nabla$ is the
Levi–Civita connection, and $\xi$ is a smooth future-directed timelike Killing
field with dimensionless components in physical length coordinates $x^0=ct$
and $x^i$ measured in metres. Put $N:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and
$u:=\xi/N$, so $g(u,u)=-1$. Its smooth
tangent-bundle data carry the supplier's explicit foundational assumption
[[def-countable-choice]] ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$); no stronger choice principle
is added here.

Let $A$ be a smooth real one-form on $O$: for each $x\in O$, $A_x:T_xO\to\mathbb R$
is linear, and in every smooth chart $(x^a)$ its coefficients $A_a$ are smooth
and obey the covector transformation law $A'_i=A_a\,\partial x^a/\partial y^i$
on an overlapping chart $(y^i)$. The coefficients have units tesla metres.
Define $F$ in each chart by
$$F_{ab}:=(dA)_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a.$$
This prescription defines a global smooth antisymmetric covariant two-tensor:
under a change of chart $x=x(y)$ the chain rule gives
$$F'_{ij}=F_{ab}\,\frac{\partial x^a}{\partial y^i}\frac{\partial x^b}{\partial y^j},$$
since the only additional term is
$A_a(\partial_i\partial_jx^a-\partial_j\partial_ix^a)=0$. Thus $F=dA$ is a two-form;
its components have units tesla. A global gauge compensator is a smooth real
function $\Lambda_\xi$ on $O$ satisfying
$$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi,\qquad (\mathcal L_\xi A)_a:=\xi^b\partial_bA_a+A_b\partial_a\xi^b$$
in every smooth chart. This defines the Lie-derivative coefficients globally:
under $x=x(y)$, put $J^a_i:=\partial x^a/\partial y^i$ and
$K^i_a:=\partial y^i/\partial x^a$. Substitution of
$A'_i=A_aJ^a_i$ and $\xi'^i=K^i_a\xi^a$ gives
$$ (\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=\xi^b(\partial_bA_a)J^a_i+\xi^bA_aK^j_b\partial_jJ^a_i+A_cJ^c_j(\partial_iK^j_b)\xi^b+A_bJ^a_i\partial_a\xi^b. $$
Differentiating $J^c_jK^j_b=\delta^c_b$ and using
$\partial_jJ^a_i=\partial_iJ^a_j$ cancels the two middle terms, leaving
$(\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=(\mathcal L_\xi A)_aJ^a_i$. The units of
$\Lambda_\xi$ are
tesla metres. No global compensator is assumed to exist for an arbitrary
smooth $A$. Define contraction by $(\iota_\xi F)_a:=\xi^bF_{ba}$.
When a global smooth compensator $\Lambda_\xi:O\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi$ is supplied as additional data, set
$$\Psi_\xi:=\xi^aA_a-\Lambda_\xi,\qquad \Phi_\xi:=-c\Psi_\xi.$$
Thus $\Psi_\xi$ has units tesla metres and $\Phi_\xi$ has units volts.
These two scalars are defined only for such supplied compensated data;

$w:=dx/ds_m$, $g(w,w)=-1$, energy four-vector $P:=Mw$, and equation

statement.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The displayed definitions give $u=k_BT\beta$ and $k_BT=(-g(\beta,\beta))^{-1/2}$, so $u=\beta/\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}$ is future unit timelike and $\beta=u/(k_BT)$. Applying the exact equivalence [F2] to this $u$ and $T$ gives the four displayed kinematic conditions if and only if $\beta$ is Killing. No hypersurface-orthogonality or zero-vorticity condition is added.

In the Killing subcase of the Statement, fix any constant $T_*>0$ kelvins and set $\xi:=k_BT_*\beta$. This is a smooth future-timelike Killing field with dimensionless components. Its lapse is $N_\xi=k_BT_*\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}=T_*/T$, so $\xi/N_\xi=u$ and $N_\xi T=T_*$. Therefore these fields satisfy the stationary thermal-carrier hypotheses of [F4], and [A3] supplies its massive-shell ansatz. That theorem states that stationarity is equivalent to $\beta$ being Killing and $d\zeta=-cq_{\rm SI}\omega$. Since this subcase already has $\beta$ Killing, its differential condition is exactly $d\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\omega$ by [A1]. This identifies the transport equation as the charged stationarity condition, without assuming stationarity in the separate solvability argument below. The only inherited set-theoretic premise is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in [F9]; no stronger choice principle is invoked.

Since $q_{\rm eff}\ne0$, any global solution of $d\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\omega$ gives $\omega=d(\alpha/q_{\rm eff})$, which is exact by [F5]. Conversely, if $\omega=d\psi$ for a global smooth $\psi$, choosing $\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\psi$ solves the equation, and $\mu=-k_BT\alpha$ is a smooth global chemical-potential scalar with the stated units. Thus the scalar transport equation has a global solution exactly when $\omega$ is exact. This is a solvability result and does not itself assert that the supplied fields are stationary.

If $\xi=k_BT_*\beta$ has the global compensator in the Statement, [F8] gives $\iota_\xi F=-d\Psi_\xi$. Since $\beta=\xi/(k_BT_*)$, we get $\omega=-(k_BT_*)^{-1}d\Psi_\xi$, an exact one-form; [F7] then forces every period to vanish. This stronger potential-symmetry condition is separate from the obstruction hypotheses.
If any closed curve has $\operatorname{Per}_\gamma(\omega)\ne0$, [F7] contradicts the exactness forced by step 1.3. Hence no global smooth charged chemical scalar can solve the transport equation.

In the rotating Minkowski model, $\partial_{x^0}$ and the smooth rotation generator $\partial_\phi=-y\partial_x+x\partial_y$ are Killing because the metric is invariant under time translations and rotations. Their constant linear combination $\beta$ is Killing and $g(\beta,\beta)=-b^2+b^2\Omega^2r^2=-b^2(1-\Omega^2r^2)$. Also $g(\beta,\partial_{x^0})=-b<0$, so it is future-directed in the stated time orientation wherever it is timelike. Thus its future-timelike domain is exactly $1-\Omega^2r^2>0$. Substituting this norm into [F1] gives the stated temperature; when $\Omega=0$ the norm is $-b^2$ for every $r$.

derivations.claim: The chosen radius satisfies $\Omega^2r^2=(1\,\mathrm{m}^{-1})^2(\tfrac12\,\mathrm m)^2=1/4$, so $\sqrt{1-\Omega^2r^2}=\sqrt3/2$ and the rotating temperature formula in [F1] gives $T=2\,\mathrm J/(\sqrt3 k_B)$. The form $\eta$ is smooth because $r^2=x^2+y^2>0$. Its coefficients are $\eta_x=-y/r^2$ and $\eta_y=x/r^2$, with $\partial_x\eta_y=(y^2-x^2)/r^4=\partial_y\eta_x$, so $d\eta=0$. Also $\eta(\partial_\phi)=(-y/r^2)(-y)+(x/r^2)x=1$. Hence $dA=C_0dx^0\wedge\eta=F$, and contraction gives $\omega=\iota_\beta F=bC_0(\eta-\Omega dx^0)$. Since $d\eta=0$ and $d(dx^0)=0$, $d\omega=0$.

For $\gamma(s)=(x^0_0,r\cos(2\pi s),r\sin(2\pi s),z_0)$, $0\le s\le1$, its tangent satisfies $dx^0(\dot\gamma)=0$ and direct substitution into $\eta=(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/r^2$ gives $\eta_{\gamma(s)}(\dot\gamma(s))=2\pi$. Hence $\operatorname{Per}_\gamma(\omega)=\int_0^1 2\pi bC_0\,ds=2\pi bC_0\ne0$.
